Surah 105: The Elephant (al-Fil)

Meccan, and its verses are 5. "It was revealed after al-Kafirun."

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is related that Abraha ibn al-Sabah al-Ashram, the king of Yemen on behalf of Ashama al-Najashi (the Negus), built a church in Sana'a and named it al-Qulays [[His saying "and named it al-Qulays," with the letter lam doubled, like al-Qubayt: a church in Sana'a belonging to the Abyssinians, built by Abraha and demolished by Himyar, as stated in al-Sihah. (ʿA)]], and he wanted to divert the pilgrims to it. A man from Kinana went and sat in it at night [[His saying "sat in it at night" is a euphemism for defecating. In al-Khazin: he defecated in it and smeared its qibla with filth. (ʿA)]], and this angered him. It was also said that a company of Arabs lit a fire which the wind carried and burned it, so he swore that he would surely demolish the Ka'ba. He set out with the Abyssinians, with an elephant named Mahmud, which was strong and huge, and with twelve other elephants. It is also said there were eight.

It was also said that he had a thousand elephants and was alone. When he reached al-Mughammis, Abd al-Muttalib went out to him and offered him a third of the wealth of Tihama in return for turning back, but he refused, arrayed his army, and sent the elephant forward. Whenever they directed it toward the Sacred Precinct it knelt and would not move, and whenever they directed it toward Yemen or any other direction it hurried. Then God sent birds, black, and it is said green, and it is said white, each bird carrying a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet, larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he saw some of these stones at Umm Hani's house, about a qafiz's worth, striped with red like Zafari onyx. The stone would fall on a man's head and come out through his backside, and each stone bore the name of the one it was to strike. They fled and perished on every road and watering place. Abraha was afflicted with a disease [[His saying "was afflicted" means he became ill, and "arabuhu" means his limbs (ʿA)]], and his fingers and limbs fell off, and he did not die until his chest split open and his heart showed. His vizier Abu Yaksum escaped, with a bird hovering over him, until he reached the Negus and recounted the story to him. When he finished it, a stone fell on him and he dropped dead before him. It is said that Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ by forty years, and it is said by twenty-three years [[His saying "by forty years, and it is said by twenty-three years": perhaps it is "and it was forty years before him." In al-Khazin: they differed about the Year of the Elephant; it is said it was forty years before the birth of the Prophet ﷺ. (ʿA)]]. It is related from ʿAʾisha, may God be pleased with her: "I saw the leader of the elephant and its driver, both blind and crippled, begging for food." And in it: Abraha had taken two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib, so he went out to him for them, and he impressed him, for he was a tall and handsome man [[His saying "he impressed him": in the Qamus, "jahira al-rajul" means his appearance was great in his eye and his beauty startled him, and "ajhara" has the same sense (ʿA)]].

It is also said: this was the chief of Quraysh and the lord of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. When he mentioned his need, Abraha said: "You have fallen from my eyes. I came to demolish the House which is your religion and your forefathers' religion, and your protection and your honour since ancient times, and a few camels taken from you have diverted you from it." He replied: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." Then he returned, came to the door of the House, took hold of its ring, and said:

O God, a man defends his household, so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their devices prevail over Your devices.
If You leave them and our Ka'ba, then do as You see fit.

[[O God, a man defends his household, so defend Your sanctuary.
And grant victory over the people of the cross and those who worship them today, Your family.
Let not their cross and their devices prevail over Your devices.
They have gathered all their lands and the elephant to take Your dependents captive.
They have aimed at Your sanctuary with their guile, in ignorance, and did not fear Your majesty.
If You leave them and our Ka'ba, then do as You see fit.

To Abd al-Muttalib, when Abraha ibn al-Sabah wished to demolish the Ka'ba and raided his two hundred camels. Abd al-Muttalib went out in search of the camels, and it had been said to Abraha that he was the lord of Quraysh, who feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain tops. When he sought the camels, Abraha said to him: "You have fallen from my eyes. I came to demolish your honour," and his concern for property diverted him from it. He said: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." Then he returned, took hold of the ring of the door, and said that. "Allahumma" has been shortened to "Lahumma." "Inna al-mar'a yamna'" means he preserves his household, and You are God, so preserve Your sanctuary, that is, the inhabitants of Your sanctuary who dwell in it. One says "hayy halal," meaning a camp, and there are many of them. Or those who are in a state of lawful residence under You. It is permissible, though remote, that he applied "halal" to the House, or its people, by way of figurative correspondence to "ahl," meaning the wife. It is also related: "Inna al-mar'a yamna'u hallahu, fa-mna' halalaka" ("A man protects his lawful possession, so protect Your sanctuary"). "Al-hall" and "al-halal" are what is lawful to dispose of. It is also related: "Inna al-'abda yamna' wahlahu, fa-mna' wahalaka," which supports the first reading. "Al" is not added except to one of noble standing, so its addition to "al-salib" is for the sake of rhyme with what follows, or according to their claim that he is of noble standing. "Wa'abidihi" is a plural whose pronoun is genitive, as a descriptive attribution to its object. "Al-yawm" is a temporal adverb of victory. "Al-mahal" is the verbal noun of "mahalahu," meaning he schemed against him with deceit. "Al-'adw" means aggression and injustice, and it is in the accusative as a specification, or as an absolute object. It is also reported as "ghadaw," meaning "tomorrow," so it is an adverb. It is also reported as "abadan," and as "juma'" in place of "jami'." There were twelve elephants with them, among them a huge, great elephant named Mahmud, so by "the elephant" is meant the species or the known one. "Al-'iyal" is its singular "'ayl," and its plural is "'ayA'il," like "jayd" and "jiyad" and "jayA'id," from the phrase "and he attends to its affairs." "'Amadu": they intended. "Hamaka," that is, Your sanctuary which You protected, because of their ignorance; or they were ignorant and did not fear Your greatness. "If You leave them with our Ka'ba, they will do with it what they wish, then it is a great matter that has appeared to You from our sins now," or a matter that You know and we do not know, of wisdom and benefit. In this is a committing of the matter to God and submission to Him.]]

O Lord, I do not hope for them to be our protection, O Lord, so defend Your sanctuary from them.
Indeed the enemy of the House is an enemy of Yours, so prevent them from destroying its courtyard.

Also to Abd al-Muttalib: that is, I do not hope to repel the enemies from us except by You. The alif at the rhyme is for lengthening, and the repetition of the address is for entreaty. "Al-'aduw" applies to the singular and the plural: whoever is an enemy to the people of Your House is an enemy to You, the utmost in enmity. "Al-fina'" is the courtyard of the House. It is related with "qura-ka" in its place, plural of "qarya," and the second hemistich beginning with a connective alif is permissible, since it is a place of beginning in general, as al-Khalil noted.]]

He turned while praying, and behold, a bird came from the direction of Yemen. He said: "By God, it is a strange bird; it is neither of the sea nor of Tihama." [[His saying "it is neither of the sea nor of Tihama": "bahriyya," in Abu al-Su'ud, is "najdiyya." (ʿA)]] And in it: the people of Mecca had hidden their wealth, and Abd al-Muttalib gathered from their jewels and gold the saddlebags [[His saying "the saddlebags": perhaps "al-jirab," plural of "jirab," like "kutub," plural of "kitab." (ʿA)]], and this was the cause of his wealth. It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him, that he was asked about the birds and said: "The pigeons of Mecca are of them." It is also said they came in the evening and then attacked them at dawn. It is related from Ikrima: whoever was struck by its pustule, which was the first smallpox to appear.

It is read "Alam tara" with the ra' sukun, for the sake of emphasis in showing the mark of the apocopating particle. The meaning: you have seen the traces of God's act against the Abyssinians, and you have heard the reports of it transmitted widely, so they stand for you in the place of direct witnessing.

"Kayfa" is in the accusative position, governed by "fa'ala Rabbuka" (your Lord did), not by "alam tara," because "kayfa" carries the meaning of interrogation. "Fi tadlil" means in wasting and nullifying. One says "dallala kaydahu" when he makes it go astray and perish. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "And the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error" [Qur'an 40:50]. Imru' al-Qays was called "al-Malik al-Dalil" because he wasted his father's kingdom, that is, lost it. Then they plotted against it a second time by intending to demolish it, so He nullified it by sending birds upon them. "Ababil" means in flocks, its singular being "ibala," and in their proverbs: "A bundle upon a bundle," which is a large bundle. The flock of birds in their crowding was likened to an "ibala." It is also said that "ababil" is like "'abadid" and "shamatit," having no singular. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, read "yarmihim" ("pelting them"), meaning God Most High or the birds, since it is a masculine collective noun, and it is feminized only according to meaning. Its derivation is from "al-isjal," which is sending, because punishment is described by that, and He sent birds upon them, and We sent upon them the flood. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "of baked clay, as bricks are baked." It is also said: it is an arabized word from "sanjakal." It is also said: from "shadid 'adhabihi" (its severe punishment). They also related the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

Striking that the warriors had enjoined upon one another as "sijjil."
[[Men who strike white swords from a crooked angle... striking that the warriors had enjoined upon one another as sijjil.

It is by Ibn Muqbil. "Rijla" is a group of men. "Al-bid" with a kasra is a metonymy for swords, meaning they strike with them; and if it is read with a fatha, it refers to the helmets on the heads of horsemen. "Al-'araj" is inclination and crookedness. It is also reported as "'an 'arad," and it is likely a distortion. The meaning is the variation of the states of striking. "Al-batal" is the brave man. "Sijjil" is the severe. But the transmission is with the nun, because the poem is in nun rhyme, and we will mention some of it at the end of the letter nun.]]

Yet it is only "sijjinan," and the poem in nun is famous in his diwan. They were compared to the leaves of a crop when eaten, that is, when the "akkal" has befallen it, which is that it is eaten by worms, or with straw eaten by beasts and trodden down; but it came according to the manner of the Qur'an's expression, as in His saying: "They both used to eat the food" [Qur'an 5:75]. Or it is intended: the grain was eaten and what remained was empty of it.

From the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah al-Fil, God will protect him during his lifetime from being swallowed up and transformed." [[Recorded by Ibn Mardawayh, al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi with a chain to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]

"Wa'abidihi" is a plural whose pronoun is genitive, as a descriptive attribution to its object. "Al-yawm" is a temporal adverb of victory. "Al-mahal" is the verbal noun of "mahalahu," meaning he schemed against him with deceit. "Al-'adw" means aggression and injustice, and it is in the accusative as a specification, or as an absolute object. It is also reported as "ghadaw," meaning "tomorrow," so it is an adverb. It is also reported as "abadan," and as "juma'" in place of "jami'." There were twelve elephants with them, among them a huge, great elephant named Mahmud, so by "the elephant" is meant the species or the known one. "Al-'iyal" is its singular "'ayl," and its plural is "'ayA'il," like "jayd" and "jiyad" and "jayA'id," from the phrase "and he attends to its affairs." "'Amadu": they intended. "Hamaka," that is, Your sanctuary which You protected, because of their ignorance; or they were ignorant and did not fear Your greatness. "If You leave them with our Ka'ba, they will do with it what they wish, then it is a great matter that has appeared to You from our sins now," or a matter that You know and we do not know, of wisdom and benefit. In this is a committing of the matter to God and submission to Him.]]

O Lord, I do not hope for them to be our protection, O Lord, so defend Your sanctuary from them.
Indeed the enemy of the House is an enemy of Yours, so prevent them from destroying its courtyard.

Also to Abd al-Muttalib: that is, I do not hope to repel the enemies from us except by You. The alif at the rhyme is for lengthening, and the repetition of the address is for entreaty. "Al-'aduw" applies to the singular and the plural: whoever is an enemy to the people of Your House is an enemy to You, the utmost in enmity. "Al-fina'" is the courtyard of the House. It is related with "qura-ka" in its place, plural of "qarya," and the second hemistich beginning with a connective alif is permissible, since it is a place of beginning in general, as al-Khalil noted.]]

He turned while praying, and behold, a bird came from the direction of Yemen. He said: "By God, it is a strange bird; it is neither of the sea nor of Tihama." [[His saying "it is neither of the sea nor of Tihama": "bahriyya," in Abu al-Su'ud, is "najdiyya." (ʿA)]] And in it: the people of Mecca had hidden their wealth, and Abd al-Muttalib gathered from their jewels and gold the saddlebags [[His saying "the saddlebags": perhaps "al-jirab," plural of "jirab," like "kutub," plural of "kitab." (ʿA)]], and this was the cause of his wealth. It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him, that he was asked about the birds and said: "The pigeons of Mecca are of them." It is also said they came in the evening and then attacked them at dawn. It is related from Ikrima: whoever was struck by its pustule, which was the first smallpox to appear.

It is read "Alam tara" with the ra' sukun, for the sake of emphasis in showing the mark of the apocopating particle. The meaning: you have seen the traces of God's act against the Abyssinians, and you have heard the reports of it transmitted widely, so they stand for you in the place of direct witnessing.

"Kayfa" is in the accusative position, governed by "fa'ala Rabbuka" (your Lord did), not by "alam tara," because "kayfa" carries the meaning of interrogation. "Fi tadlil" means in wasting and nullifying. One says "dallala kaydahu" when he makes it go astray and perish. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "And the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error" [Qur'an 40:50]. Imru' al-Qays was called "al-Malik al-Dalil" because he wasted his father's kingdom, that is, lost it. The meaning: they first plotted against the House by building al-Qulays and intended to abolish its status by turning the faces of the pilgrims toward it, so God nullified their plot by setting fire to it. Then they plotted against it a second time by intending to demolish it, so He nullified it by sending birds upon them. "Ababil" means in flocks, its singular being "ibala," and in their proverbs: "A bundle upon a bundle," which is a large bundle. The flock of birds in their crowding was likened to an "ibala." It is also said that "ababil" is like "'abadid" and "shamatit," having no singular. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, read "yarmihim" ("pelting them"), meaning God Most High or the birds, since it is a masculine collective noun, and it is feminized only according to meaning. "Sijjil" seems to be a proper name for the register in which the punishment of the disbelievers is recorded, just as "Sijjin" is the name of the register of their deeds, as if it were said: with stones from among the punishment written and recorded. Its derivation is from "al-isjal," which is sending, because punishment is described by that, and He sent birds upon them, and We sent upon them the flood. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "of baked clay, as bricks are baked." It is also said: it is an arabized word from "sanjakal." It is also said: from "shadid 'adhabihi" (its severe punishment). They also related the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

Striking that the warriors had enjoined upon one another as "sijjil."
[[Men who strike white swords from a crooked angle... striking that the warriors had enjoined upon one another as sijjil.

It is by Ibn Muqbil. "Rijla" is a group of men. "Al-bid" with a kasra is a metonymy for swords, meaning they strike with them; and if it is read with a fatha, it refers to the helmets on the heads of horsemen. "Al-'araj" is inclination and crookedness. It is also reported as "'an 'arad," and it is likely a distortion. The meaning is the variation of the states of striking. "Al-batal" is the brave man. "Sijjil" is the severe. But the transmission is with the nun, because the poem is in nun rhyme, and we will mention some of it at the end of the letter nun.]]

Yet it is only "sijjinan," and the poem in nun is famous in his diwan. They were compared to the leaves of a crop when eaten, that is, when the "akkal" has befallen it, which is that it is eaten by worms, or with straw eaten by beasts and trodden down; but it came according to the manner of the Qur'an's expression, as in His saying: "They both used to eat the food" [Qur'an 5:75]. Or it is intended: the grain was eaten and what remained was empty of it.

From the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah al-Fil, God will protect him during his lifetime from being swallowed up and transformed." [[Recorded by Ibn Mardawayh, al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi with a chain to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]
